<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Let $K$ be a finite field of characteristic two with $|K| = 2^{n}$, let
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $\gcd(k,n) = 1$, and let
$\Delta_{k} = \{\delta_{k}(b) : b \in K\}$ with
$\delta_{k}(b) = (b+1)^{d_{k}} + b^{d_{k}} + 1$ and
$d_{k} = 4^{k}-2^{k}+1$.  Then for all $v_{1},v_{2} \in K$ with
$v_{1} \neq 0$, $v_{2} \neq 0$, and $v_{1} \neq v_{2}$,
\[
  N_{k}(v_{1},v_{2}) :=
  \bigl|\{(x,y,z) \in \Delta_{k}^{3} :
     v_{1}x+v_{2}y+(v_{1}+v_{2})z=0\}\bigr| = 2^{2n-3}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:objects}
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put
\[
  d_{k} = 4^{k} - 2^{k} + 1 \in \mathbb{N},
  \qquad
  \delta_{k}(b) = (b+1)^{d_{k}} + b^{d_{k}} + 1 \quad (b \in K),
\]
\[
  \Delta_{k} = \delta_{k}(K) \subseteq K,
  \qquad
  N_{k}(v_{1},v_{2}) =
    \bigl|\{(x,y,z) \in \Delta_{k}^{3} :
        v_{1}x+v_{2}y+(v_{1}+v_{2})z = 0\}\bigr| .
\]
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:slopes}
For $\rho \in K$ set
\[
  N(\rho) = \bigl|\{(x,y,z) \in \Delta_{k}^{3} :
     x + \rho y + (1+\rho)z = 0\}\bigr|.
\]
A slope $\rho$ is \emph{admissible} if
$\rho \neq 0$ and $\rho \neq 1$; we write
$\mathcal S = \{ \rho \in K : \rho \neq 0,\ \rho \neq 1\}$.  The \emph{Walsh coefficient} of
$\Delta \subseteq K$ is
\[
  S(a) = \widehat{\mathbf{1}_{\Delta}}(a) = \sum_{x \in \Delta} \psi(ax) \qquad (a \in K),
\]
and the \emph{phase triple sum} at a pair
$(\rho,\sigma)$ is
\[
  Z(\rho) = \sum_{\lambda \in K^{\times}}
     S(\lambda) S(\rho\lambda) S(\sigma\lambda),
  \qquad \sigma = 1+\rho.
\]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:coefslope}
If $v_{1} \neq 0$ then $N_{k}(v_{1},v_{2}) = N(v_{2}/v_{1})$.  If moreover
$v_{2} \neq 0$ and $v_{1} \neq v_{2}$, then $\rho = v_{2}/v_{1}$ is admissible.
Conversely, if $N(\rho) = c$ for every admissible $\rho$, then
$N_{k}(v_{1},v_{2}) = c$ for all admissible coefficient pairs.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Dividing $v_{1}x+v_{2}y+(v_{1}+v_{2})z = 0$ by $v_{1}$ gives
$x + \rho y + (1+\rho)z = 0$ with $\rho = v_{2}/v_{1}$, and multiplication by
$v_{1} \neq 0$ is a bijection of the solution set of one equation onto the
other; the two filtered subsets of $\Delta_{k}^{3}$ are literally equal.  If
$v_{2} \neq 0$ then $\rho \neq 0$, and $v_{1} \neq v_{2}$ gives $\rho \neq 1$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- result-1: body_md -->
\label{res:halfsize}
Let $|K| = 2^{n}$, $1 \le k < n$, $\gcd(k,n) = 1$.  Then
\[
  2\,|\Delta_{k}| = |K| .
\]
<!-- end result-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
This is the half-size consequence of \cite[Theorem A]{DillonDobbertin}; see
\cite[Corollary 2]{DobbertinNATO} for a direct proof of APN-ness.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:expperiod}
For all $n,k$ one has $d_{k} \equiv d_{k \bmod n} \pmod{2^{n}-1}$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Write $k = (k \bmod n) + n\lfloor k/n\rfloor$.  Since $2^{n} \equiv 1
\pmod{2^{n}-1}$ we get $2^{k} \equiv 2^{k \bmod n}$ and, squaring,
$4^{k} \equiv 4^{k\bmod n} \pmod{2^{n}-1}$.  As $2^{j} \le 4^{j}$ for all $j$,
the truncated differences also agree modulo $2^{n}-1$, and adding $1$
preserves the congruence.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:powperiod}
Let $x \in K$ and let $a,b \ge 1$ with $a \equiv b \pmod{|K|-1}$.  Then
$x^{a} = x^{b}$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For $x = 0$ both sides vanish because $a,b \ge 1$.  For $x \neq 0$ use
$x^{|K|-1} = 1$ and split each exponent as remainder plus multiple of $|K|-1$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:reduction}
Let $|K| = 2^{n}$.  Then for every $k$,
\[
  \delta_{k} = \delta_{k \bmod n}, \qquad
  \Delta_{k} = \Delta_{k \bmod n}, \qquad
  N_{k}(v_{1},v_{2}) = N_{k \bmod n}(v_{1},v_{2}).
\]
Moreover, if $|K|=2^{n}$ and $K$ contains two distinct nonzero elements
$v_{1} \neq v_{2}$, then $n \ge 2$; and if $n \ge 2$ and $\gcd(k,n)=1$ then
$r = k \bmod n$ satisfies $1 \le r < n$ and $\gcd(r,n)=1$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
$d_{k} \ge 1$ always, so Lemmas~\ref{lem:expperiod} and~\ref{lem:powperiod}
give $x^{d_{k}} = x^{d_{k \bmod n}}$ for all $x \in K$; applying this to
$x = b+1$ and $x = b$ gives $\delta_{k} = \delta_{k \bmod n}$, and the image and
the count follow.  For the second part, $0, v_{1}, v_{2}$ are three distinct
elements, so $2^{n} = |K| \ge 3$, forcing $n \ge 2$.  Finally $\gcd(k,n)=1$
gives $\gcd(k \bmod n, n) = 1$, and $k \bmod n = 0$ would force $n = 1$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:complement}
Let $|K| = 2^{n}$ and $k \le n$.  Then for all $b \in K$,
\[
  \delta_{k}(b) = \bigl(\delta_{n-k}(b)\bigr)^{2^{2k}},
\]
so $\Delta_{k}$ is the image of $\Delta_{n-k}$ under the automorphism
$x \mapsto x^{2^{2k}}$; in particular $|\Delta_{k}| = |\Delta_{n-k}|$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
A direct computation with the Kasami exponents gives the integer identity
\[
  2^{2k}\,d_{n-k} = d_{k} + (2^{n}-1)\bigl((2^{n}-2^{k})+1\bigr),
\]
and exponents may be shifted by multiples of $|K|-1 = 2^{n}-1$ without changing
the value of $x \mapsto x^{e}$ for $e \ge 1$.  Hence
$x^{d_{n-k}2^{2k}} = x^{d_{k}}$ for all $x \in K$, and applying this to $b+1$
and $b$ and using that $x \mapsto x^{2^{2k}}$ is additive gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:walshcount}
For every $\rho \in K$,
\[
  N(\rho) = \frac{Q^{2}}{8} + \frac{ Z(\rho)}{Q}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Orthogonality of $\psi$ gives, for $t \in K$,
$\sum_{a \in K}\psi(at) = Q\cdot \mathbf 1_{t=0}$.  Hence
\[
  Q\, N(\rho)
  = \sum_{(x,y,z) \in \Delta^{3}} \ \sum_{a \in K}
      \psi\bigl(a(x+\rho y+(1+\rho)z)\bigr)
  = \sum_{a \in K} S(a)\,S(\rho a)\,S\bigl((1+\rho)a\bigr),
\]
because for fixed $a$ the character factorises over the three coordinates.
The term $a=0$ contributes $S(0)^{3} = |\Delta|^{3} = Q^{3}/8$, and the
remaining terms are by definition $Z(\rho)$.  Dividing by $Q$ gives the formula.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:average}
Assume $Q > 2$ and $2|\Delta| = Q$.  Then
\[
  \frac{1}{|\mathcal S|}\sum_{\rho \in \mathcal S} N(\rho) = \frac{Q^{2}}{8},
  \qquad \mathcal S = K \setminus\{0,1\},\quad |\mathcal S| = Q-2 .
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
We double count the set of pairs $(\rho, (x,y,z))$ with $\rho \in \mathcal S$,
$(x,y,z) \in \Delta^{3}$ and $x+\rho y+(1+\rho)z = 0$.  Fix a triple
$(x,y,z)$.

If $y = z$ the equation reads $x+y = 0$, so it holds for every admissible
$\rho$ exactly when $x=y=z$.  If $y \neq z$, the unique solution is
$\rho = (x+z)/(y+z)$, and this is admissible exactly when $x,y,z$ are pairwise
distinct.  Hence
\[
  \sum_{\rho \in \mathcal S} N(\rho)
   = (Q-2)|\Delta| + |\Delta|(|\Delta|-1)(|\Delta|-2).
\]
Substituting $|\Delta|=Q/2$ and dividing by $Q-2$ gives
\[
  \frac{1}{Q-2}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal S}N(\rho)
  = \frac{Q}{2} + \frac{Q}{2}\left(\frac{Q}{4}-1\right)
  = \frac{Q^{2}}{8}.
\]
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:normparam}
Let $k<n$ with $\gcd(k,n)=1$.  Then there are $k_{0}, m \in \mathbb{N}$ with
\[
  k_{0} \in \{k,\, n-k\}, \qquad k_{0} \text{ odd}, \qquad \gcd(k_{0},n)=1,
  \qquad 2^{k_{0}}+1 = 3m, \qquad \gcd(m, 2^{n}-1) = 1 .
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We first show that an odd $k_{0}$ coprime to $n$ works as soon as either $n$ is
odd or $k_{0}\not\equiv 3 \pmod 6$.  For odd
$k_{0}$ one has $2^{k_{0}}\equiv 2 \pmod 3$, so $3 \mid 2^{k_{0}}+1$ and
$2^{k_{0}}+1 = 3m$ for some $m$.  Since $\gcd(k_{0},n)=1$, we have
$\gcd(2^{2k_{0}}-1, 2^{n}-1) = 2^{\gcd(2k_{0},n)}-1 \in \{1,3\}$, and
$2^{k_{0}}+1 \mid 2^{2k_{0}}-1$, so every common divisor
of $2^{k_{0}}+1$ and $2^{n}-1$ divides $3$; hence $\gcd(m,2^{n}-1)$ divides $3$
as well, and equals $3$ only if $9 \mid 3m = 2^{k_{0}}+1$ and $3 \mid 2^{n}-1$.
Now $9 \mid 2^{k_{0}}+1$ holds exactly when $k_{0}\equiv 3 \pmod 6$, and $3 \mid 2^{n}-1$ exactly when
$n$ is even.  So under either of the two stated conditions
$\gcd(m,2^{n}-1)=1$.

It remains to choose $k_{0}\in\{k,n-k\}$ accordingly; in both cases
$1 \le k_{0} < n$ and $\gcd(k_{0},n) = \gcd(k,n) = 1$.  If $n$ is odd, exactly
one of $k$, $n-k$ is odd, and we take that one; no residue condition is needed.
If $n$ is even, then $k$ and $n-k$ are both odd; if $k \not\equiv 3 \pmod 6$ we
take $k_{0}=k$, and otherwise $3 \mid k$, so $3 \nmid n$ by coprimality, hence
$n \equiv 2$ or $4 \pmod 6$ and $n-k \equiv 5$ or $1 \pmod 6$; in particular
$n-k \not\equiv 3 \pmod 6$ and we take $k_{0}=n-k$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:transport}
Let $|K|=2^{n}$, $k \le n$, and let $v_{1},v_{2}$ be distinct nonzero
elements.  Then there are distinct nonzero $w_{1},w_{2}$ with
\[
  N_{k}(v_{1},v_{2}) = N_{n-k}(w_{1},w_{2}).
\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:complement}, $\Delta_{k} = \phi(\Delta_{n-k})$ where
$\phi(x) = x^{2^{2k}}$ is a field automorphism.  Applying $\phi^{-1}$ to a
solution triple of $v_{1}x+v_{2}y+(v_{1}+v_{2})z=0$ in $\Delta_{k}^{3}$ gives a
solution triple in $\Delta_{n-k}^{3}$ of the equation with coefficients
$w_{i} = \phi^{-1}(v_{i})$, and this is a bijection between the two solution
sets.  Distinctness and nonvanishing are preserved by $\phi^{-1}$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
It is important that the transport moves the \emph{coefficients}: it is
\emph{not} true that $N(\rho)$ at parameter $k$ equals $N(\rho)$ at parameter
$n-k$ for the same slope $\rho$.  Frobenius acts on the slope too.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:phase}
Assume \eqref{eq:normalized}.  Then for every multiplicative character $\chi$
of $K$,
\[
  \widehat F(\chi)
   = \frac{G(\chi)\,G\bigl(\chi^{2^{k}+1}\bigr)}{G\bigl(\chi^{3}\bigr)} .
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
This is the formula of Dillon and Kashyap~\cite[Theorems 1--2]{DillonKashyap},
after changing their sign convention because their difference set is the
complement of $\Delta$.  The displayed expression is well defined:
$G(\chi^{3}) \neq 0$ for every $\chi$ because $\psi$ is primitive; see Lemma \ref{lem:gauss-sum}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:gauss-sum}
For a multiplicative character $\chi: K^{\times} \to \mathbb{C}^{\times}$, let
\[ G(\chi) = \sum_{x \in K^{\times}} \chi(x) \psi(x) \]
be its Gauss sum. Then $G(1)=-1$ and $G(\chi)G(\chi^{-1}) = Q$ for nontrivial $\chi$. Moreover, the multiplicative Fourier inversion formula
\[ \sum_\chi G(\chi^{-1}) \chi(x) = (Q-1) \psi(x)\]
holds for all $x \in K^{\times}$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
For the trivial character $1$, we have $G(1) = \sum_{x \in K^{\times}} \psi(x) = -1$ because $\sum_{x \in K} \psi(x) = 0$ and $\psi(0) = 1$. Fix a nontrivial character $\chi$. Then
  \begin{align*}
    G(\chi)G(\chi^{-1}) &= \sum_{x \in K^{\times}} \sum_{y \in K^{\times}} \chi(x) \chi^{-1}(y) \psi(x) \psi(y) \\
    & = \sum_{x,y \in K^{\times}} \chi(x/y) \psi(x+y) \\
    & = \sum_{y,u \in K^{\times}} \chi(u) \psi(y(u+1)) \quad \text{with } u = x/y \\
    & = \chi(1) \sum_{y \in K^{\times}} \psi(0) + \sum_{u \neq 0,1} \chi(u) \sum_{y\in K^{\times}} \psi(y(u+1)) \\
    & = 1\cdot (2^n-1) - \sum_{u \neq 0,1} \chi(u)  \\
    & = 2^n -\sum_{u \in K^{\times}} \chi(u) = 2^n = Q.
  \end{align*}
  For the multiplicative Fourier inversion formula, 
  \begin{align*}
    \sum_\chi G(\chi^{-1}) \chi(x) &= \sum_\chi \sum_{y \in K^{\times}} \chi^{-1}(y) \psi(y) \chi(x) \\
    &=\sum_{y \in K^{\times}} \psi(y) \sum_\chi \chi(x/y) \\
    &= (Q-1) \psi(x),
  \end{align*}
  where we used the orthogonality of characters: $\sum_\chi \chi(x) = 2^n-1$ if $x=1$ and $0$ otherwise.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:walshchar}
Assume \eqref{eq:normalized} and put $e = 2^{k}+1$.  Then for every
$a \in K^{\times}$,
\[
  2\,S(a) = \frac{Q}{N}\sum_{\chi}
      \frac{G(\chi^{e})}{G(\chi^{3})}\,\chi(a),
\]
the sum ranging over all $N = |K^{\times}|$ multiplicative characters of $K$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
On $K^{\times}$ we have $1_{\Delta} = (1+F)/2$, so by \eqref{eq:zeroinDelta}
\[
  2S(a) = 2\sum_{x \in \Delta}\psi(ax)
        = 2 + \sum_{x \in K^{\times}}\bigl(1+F(x)\bigr)\psi(ax)
        = 1 + \sum_{x\inK^{\times}}F(x)\psi(ax),
\]
using $\sum_{x \in K^{\times}}\psi(ax) = -1$ for $a \neq 0$.  Multiplicative
Fourier inversion on $K^{\times}$ (Lemma \ref{lem:gauss-sum}) turns the last sum into
\[
  \sum_{x\inK^{\times}}F(x)\psi(ax)
   = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\chi}\widehat F(\chi)\,\chi(a)\,G(\chi^{-1}),
\]
and inserting Theorem~\ref{thm:phase} together with
$G(\chi)G(\chi^{-1}) = Q$ for $\chi \neq 1$ and $G(1) = -1$ converts each term
into $\frac{Q}{N}\frac{G(\chi^{e})}{G(\chi^{3})}\chi(a)$, except for the
principal character, whose correction is exactly the constant $1$ subtracted
above.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:rootcount}
Let $\mu_{3} = \{u \in K : u^{3}=1\}$ and $c = |\mu_{3}| \in \{1,3\}$; $c=3$
if $n$ is even and $c=1$ if $n$ is odd.  Put
\[
  \Phi(x) = \sum_{u \in \mu_{3}}\psi\bigl(u x^{D}\bigr),
  \qquad
  \widehat\Phi(z) = \sum_{t \in K}\Phi(t)\psi(zt),
\]
\[
  W_{u,v}(A,B) = \sum_{x,y \in K}
      \psi\bigl(u x^{D} + v (Ax+By)^{D} + y^{D}\bigr),
\]
\[
  R_{u,v}(A,B) = \bigl|\{t \in K : u t^{D} + v (At+B)^{D} = 1\}\bigr| .
\]
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:phaseroot}
Let $\psi$ be primitive, $e = 3m$, $mD \equiv 1 \pmod N$, and let
$S \colon K \to \mathbb{C}$ satisfy the all-character Walsh formula of
Theorem~\ref{thm:walshchar}.  Let $A,B \in K$ with $A \neq 0$,
$A^{3}+B^{3} = 1$, and $A^{3}\neq 1$.  Then
\[
  Z(A^{3})
  = \frac{Q^{2}}{8}\Bigl(
      \sum_{u,v \in \mu_{3}} R_{u,v}(A,B) - c^{2}\Bigr),
\]
where $Z$ is the phase triple sum at the pair $(\rho,\sigma) = (A^{3},B^{3})$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:powD}
Let $m,D \ge 1$ with $mD \equiv 1 \pmod{N}$.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x^{mD} = x$ for every $x \in K$; consequently $(x^{D})^{m} = x$ and
  $(x^{m})^{D} = x$, so $x \mapsto x^{D}$ and $x \mapsto x^{m}$ are mutually
  inverse bijections of $K$ fixing $0$ and $1$;
\item for every $C \in K$,
  \[
    \sum_{y \in K}\psi\bigl(C y^{D}\bigr) =
      \begin{cases} Q, & C = 0,\\ 0, & C \neq 0.\end{cases}
  \]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
(1) Write $mD = 1 + Nj$ with $j \ge 0$, which is possible since
$mD \ge 1$ and $mD \equiv 1 \pmod N$.  For $x = 0$ the claim is
$0^{mD} = 0$, true because $mD \ge 1$.  For $x \in K^{\times}$ we have $x^{N} = 1$ by
Lagrange, so $x^{mD} = x\cdot (x^{N})^{j} = x$.  Since $mD = Dm$, both
$(x^{D})^{m} = x$ and $(x^{m})^{D} = x$ follow, which exhibits the two maps as
mutually inverse.

(2) By (1) the substitution $y = x^{m}$, i.e.\ $x = y^{D}$, is a bijection of
$K$, so $\sum_{y}\psi(Cy^{D}) = \sum_{x}\psi(Cx)$.  The latter is the sum of
the shifted character $\psi_{C} = \psi(C\,\cdot\,)$ over the additive group $K$;
it equals $Q$ if $\psi_{C}$ is trivial and $0$ otherwise, and by primitivity of
$\psi$ the character $\psi_{C}$ is trivial exactly for $C = 0$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:mu3basic}
$\mu_{3} = \{u \in K : u^{3} = 1\}$ is a subgroup of $K^{\times}$ of order
$c = \gcd(3,Q-1)$; thus $c = 3$ if $n$ is even and $c = 1$ if $n$ is odd, and
in particular $c \neq 0$.  Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}
\item for every $A \in K^{\times}$ the fibre of the cubing map through $A$ is
  $\{b \in K^{\times} : b^{3} = A^{3}\} = A\mu_{3}$, of cardinality exactly $c$;
\item if $c = 1$ then every element of $K^{\times}$ is a cube;
\item $u \mapsto (u^{-1})^{D}$ is a bijection of $\mu_{3}$ onto itself, with
  inverse $v \mapsto (v^{m})^{-1}$;
\item for $b \in \mu_{3}$, both $a \mapsto ab^{-1}$ and $g \mapsto gb^{-1}$
  are bijections of $\mu_{3}$ onto itself.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
$\mu_{3}$ is the kernel of the endomorphism $x \mapsto x^{3}$ of the cyclic
group $K^{\times}$ of order $N = Q-1$, hence a subgroup of order $\gcd(3,N)$.  Since
$Q = 2^{n}$ and $2 \equiv -1 \pmod 3$, we get $3 \mid 2^{n}-1$ iff $n$ is even.
(1) is the coset description of a kernel fibre: $b^{3} = A^{3}$ iff
$(bA^{-1})^{3} = 1$ iff $b \in A\mu_{3}$, and $b \mapsto bA^{-1}$ is a
bijection $A\mu_{3} \to \mu_{3}$.  (2) If $c=1$ the cubing map is injective
on the finite group $K^{\times}$, hence surjective.  (3) If $u^{3} = 1$ then
$((u^{-1})^{D})^{3} = ((u^{3})^{-1})^{D} = 1$, so the map sends $\mu_{3}$ into
itself.  Writing $\varphi(u) = (u^{-1})^{D}$ and $\varphi'(v) = (v^{m})^{-1}$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:powD}(1) gives
$\varphi'(\varphi(u)) = \bigl(((u^{-1})^{D})^{m}\bigr)^{-1} = (u^{-1})^{-1} = u$
and
$\varphi(\varphi'(v)) = \bigl(((v^{m})^{-1})^{-1}\bigr)^{D} = (v^{m})^{D} = v$,
so the two maps are mutually inverse bijections of $\mu_{3}$.  (4) is the
bijectivity of translation in a group.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:ratio}
For every multiplicative character $\chi$ of $K$, with $\theta = \chi^{3}$,
\[
  \frac{G(\chi^{3m})}{G(\chi^{3})}
   = \frac{G(\theta^{m})\,G(\theta^{-1})}{Q}
     + \begin{cases} 1 - \dfrac1Q, & \theta = 1,\\[2pt] 0, & \theta \neq 1 .\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Both sides are well defined because $G(\theta) \neq 0$ for every $\theta$.
If $\theta = 1$ then also
$\theta^{m} = 1$ and $\theta^{-1} = 1$, so the left-hand side is
$G(1)/G(1) = 1$ while the right-hand side is
$G(1)^{2}/Q + 1 - 1/Q = 1/Q + 1 - 1/Q = 1$, using $G(1) = -1$.  If
$\theta \neq 1$ then $G(\theta)G(\theta^{-1}) = Q$, i.e.\
$G(\theta^{-1})/Q = G(\theta)^{-1}$, and the right-hand side is
$G(\theta^{m})/G(\theta)$, which is the left-hand side.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:gaussprod}
For every $a \in K^{\times}$,
\[
  \sum_{\chi} G\bigl((\chi^{3})^{m}\bigr)\,G\bigl((\chi^{3})^{-1}\bigr)\,\chi(a)
   = N \sum_{x \in K^{\times}}\ \sum_{\substack{y \in K^{\times}\\ y^{3} = a\,x^{3m}}}\psi(x+y).
\]
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Expand both Gauss sums as sums over $K^{\times}$ (legitimate since $\chi(0)=0$):
\[
  G\bigl((\chi^{3})^{m}\bigr)G\bigl((\chi^{3})^{-1}\bigr)\chi(a)
   = \sum_{x \in K^{\times}}\sum_{y \in K^{\times}}
      \chi^{3m}(x)\,\chi^{-3}(y)\,\chi(a)\,\psi(x)\psi(y).
\]
Since $\chi$ is multiplicative and $\psi(x)\psi(y) = \psi(x+y)$, the summand
equals $\chi\bigl(x^{3m}y^{-3}a\bigr)\psi(x+y)$.  Summing over all $\chi$ and
interchanging the (finite) sums, the first orthogonality relation
\[
  \sum_{\chi}\chi(g) = \begin{cases} N, & g = 1,\\ 0, & g \neq 1\end{cases}
  \qquad (g \in K^{\times})
\]
gives
\[
  \sum_{\chi}G\bigl((\chi^{3})^{m}\bigr)G\bigl((\chi^{3})^{-1}\bigr)\chi(a)
   = N \sum_{\substack{x,y \in K^{\times}\\ x^{3m}y^{-3}a = 1}}\psi(x+y).
\]
Finally $x^{3m}y^{-3}a = 1$ is equivalent to $y^{3} = a\,x^{3m}$, which is the
indexing of the asserted inner sum.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:closedform}
For every $a \in K^{\times}$,
\[
  2S(a) = \bigl|\{b \in K^{\times} : b^{3} = a\}\bigr|
        + \sum_{x \in K^{\times}}\ \sum_{\substack{y \in K^{\times}\\ y^{3} = a x^{3m}}}
          \psi(x+y) .
\]
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Insert Lemma~\ref{lem:ratio} into \eqref{eq:walshhyp} and split the resulting
sum into the two contributions.  The first contributes
\[
  \frac{Q}{N}\cdot\frac1Q
    \sum_{\chi}G\bigl((\chi^{3})^{m}\bigr)G\bigl((\chi^{3})^{-1}\bigr)\chi(a)
  = \frac1N \cdot N\sum_{x \in K^{\times}}\sum_{\substack{y\inK^{\times}\\ y^{3}=ax^{3m}}}
      \psi(x+y)
\]
by Lemma~\ref{lem:gaussprod}, i.e.\ exactly the double sum in the statement.
The second contributes
\[
  \frac{Q}{N}\Bigl(1-\frac1Q\Bigr)\sum_{\chi^{3}=1}\chi(a)
   = \frac{Q-1}{N}\sum_{\chi^{3}=1}\chi(a)
   = \sum_{\chi^{3}=1}\chi(a),
\]
because $N = Q-1$.  It remains to identify $\sum_{\chi^{3}=1}\chi(a)$ with the
number of cube roots of $a$ in $K^{\times}$.  This is the standard count: by the two
orthogonality relations,
\[
  N\,\bigl|\{b : b^{3}=a\}\bigr|
   = \sum_{b \in K^{\times}}\sum_{\chi}\chi\bigl(b^{3}a^{-1}\bigr)
   = \sum_{\chi}\Bigl(\sum_{b\inK^{\times}}\chi^{3}(b)\Bigr)\chi(a^{-1})
   = N\sum_{\chi^{3}=1}\chi(a^{-1}),
\]
since $\sum_{b}\chi^{3}(b)$ is $N$ or $0$ according as $\chi^{3} = 1$ or not.
Dividing by $N$ and using that $\chi \mapsto \chi^{-1}$ is an involution of the
set $\{\chi : \chi^{3}=1\}$ with $\chi^{-1}(a^{-1}) = \chi(a)$, we get
$\sum_{\chi^{3}=1}\chi(a) = |\{b \in K^{\times}: b^{3}=a\}|$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:Snoncube}
If $a \in K^{\times}$ is not a cube in $K^{\times}$, then $S(a) = 0$.  (This is vacuous when
$c=1$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:mu3basic}(2).)
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Both terms of Lemma~\ref{lem:closedform} vanish.  The first is the number of
cube roots of $a$, which is $0$ by hypothesis.  For the second, fix
$x \in K^{\times}$ and suppose $y \in K^{\times}$ satisfies $y^{3} = a\,x^{3m}$.  Then
\[
  \bigl(y\,(x^{m})^{-1}\bigr)^{3} = y^{3}\,x^{-3m} = a,
\]
so $a$ would be a cube, a contradiction; hence every inner index set is empty.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:twoScube}
For every $A \in K^{\times}$,
\[
  2S(A^{3}) = \widehat\Phi(A) = \sum_{t \in K}\Phi(t)\,\psi(At).
\]
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:closedform} with $a = A^{3}$.

\emph{First term.}  By Lemma~\ref{lem:mu3basic}(1) the number of cube roots of
$A^{3}$ in $K^{\times}$ is exactly $c$.

\emph{Second term.}  Fix $x \in K^{\times}$.  The set
$\{y \in K^{\times} : y^{3} = A^{3}x^{3m}\}$ is the fibre of the cubing map through
$Ax^{m}$, hence equals $\{u\,A\,x^{m} : u \in \mu_{3}\}$, again by
Lemma~\ref{lem:mu3basic}(1); the parametrisation $u \mapsto uAx^{m}$ is
injective.  Therefore
\[
  \sum_{\substack{y\inK^{\times}\\ y^{3}=A^{3}x^{3m}}}\psi(x+y)
   = \sum_{u \in \mu_{3}}\psi\bigl(x + uAx^{m}\bigr),
\]
and, interchanging the two finite sums,
\[
  2S(A^{3}) = c + \sum_{u \in \mu_{3}}\ \sum_{x \in K^{\times}}
     \psi\bigl(x+uAx^{m}\bigr).
\]

\emph{Restoring the point $x=0$.}  Since $m \ge 1$, the summand at $x = 0$ is
$\psi(0) = 1$ for each $u$, so
$\sum_{x\in K} = 1 + \sum_{x \in K^{\times}}$ termwise in $u$, and the $c$ ones
produced this way absorb the leading constant $c$:
\[
  2S(A^{3}) = \sum_{u \in \mu_{3}}\ \sum_{x \in K}\psi\bigl(x+uAx^{m}\bigr).
\]

\emph{Substitution.}  Fix $u \in \mu_{3}$ and put $\tau_{u} = (u^{-1})^{D}$,
which is nonzero.  The map $t \mapsto \tau_{u}t^{D}$ is a bijection of $K$,
being the composition of the bijection $t \mapsto t^{D}$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:powD}(1)) with multiplication by $\tau_{u} \neq 0$.  Writing
$x = \tau_{u}t^{D}$ we get, by Lemma~\ref{lem:powD}(1) again,
\[
  x^{m} = \bigl(\tau_{u}\bigr)^{m}\bigl(t^{D}\bigr)^{m}
        = u^{-1}\,t ,
  \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
  uAx^{m} = A\,t .
\]
Therefore
\[
  \sum_{x \in K}\psi\bigl(x+uAx^{m}\bigr)
   = \sum_{t \in K}\psi\bigl(\tau_{u}t^{D} + At\bigr).
\]

\emph{Reindexing $\mu_{3}$.}  By Lemma~\ref{lem:mu3basic}(3),
$u \mapsto \tau_{u} = (u^{-1})^{D}$ permutes $\mu_{3}$, so
\[
  2S(A^{3}) = \sum_{v \in \mu_{3}}\sum_{t \in K}\psi\bigl(vt^{D}+At\bigr)
   = \sum_{t \in K}\Bigl(\sum_{v \in \mu_{3}}\psi\bigl(vt^{D}\bigr)\Bigr)\psi(At)
   = \sum_{t\in K}\Phi(t)\psi(At) = \widehat\Phi(A),
\]
where the middle equality is $\psi(\alpha+\beta) = \psi(\alpha)\psi(\beta)$ and
an interchange of two finite sums.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:eightZ}
Let $A,B \in K^{\times}$.  Then
\[
  8\,Z(A^{3})\cdot c
   = \sum_{z \in K^{\times}}\widehat\Phi(z)\,\widehat\Phi(Az)\,\widehat\Phi(Bz),
\]
where $Z(A^{3})$ is the phase triple sum at $(\rho,\sigma) = (A^{3},B^{3})$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Put $f(\lambda) = 8\,S(\lambda)S(A^{3}\lambda)S(B^{3}\lambda)$ for
$\lambda \in K^{\times}$, so that $8Z(A^{3}) = \sum_{\lambda \in K^{\times}}f(\lambda)$ by
the definition of the phase triple sum.

\emph{Values at cubes.}  For $z \in K^{\times}$ we have
$A^{3}z^{3} = (Az)^{3}$ and $B^{3}z^{3} = (Bz)^{3}$, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:twoScube} applied at the three units $z$, $Az$, $Bz$,
\[
  f(z^{3}) = \bigl(2S(z^{3})\bigr)\bigl(2S((Az)^{3})\bigr)\bigl(2S((Bz)^{3})\bigr)
     = \widehat\Phi(z)\widehat\Phi(Az)\widehat\Phi(Bz).
\]

\emph{Fibrewise counting.}  Sorting the sum $\sum_{z \in K^{\times}}f(z^{3})$ by the
value $\lambda = z^{3}$,
\[
  \sum_{z \in K^{\times}}f(z^{3})
   = \sum_{\lambda \in K^{\times}}\bigl|\{z \in K^{\times} : z^{3}=\lambda\}\bigr|\,f(\lambda).
\]
For each $\lambda$ we claim
$|\{z : z^{3}=\lambda\}|\,f(\lambda) = c\,f(\lambda)$.  Indeed, if $\lambda$ is
a cube the cardinality is $c$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:mu3basic}(1); and if $\lambda$
is not a cube then $S(\lambda) = 0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:Snoncube}, so
$f(\lambda) = 0$ and both sides vanish.  Hence
\[
  \sum_{z\inK^{\times}}\widehat\Phi(z)\widehat\Phi(Az)\widehat\Phi(Bz)
   = \sum_{z\inK^{\times}}f(z^{3})
   = c\sum_{\lambda\inK^{\times}}f(\lambda)
   = 8\,Z(A^{3})\,c . \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:phihatzero}
$\sum_{t \in K}\Phi(t) = 0$, and consequently $\widehat\Phi(0) = 0$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Interchanging the two sums and using Lemma~\ref{lem:powD}(2) for each
$u \in \mu_{3}$, which is nonzero,
\[
  \sum_{t\in K}\Phi(t) = \sum_{u \in \mu_{3}}\sum_{t \in K}\psi\bigl(ut^{D}\bigr)
   = \sum_{u \in \mu_{3}}0 = 0 .
\]
Since $\psi(0\cdot t) = 1$, this is precisely $\widehat\Phi(0)$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:parseval}
For all $A,B \in K$,
\[
  \sum_{z\in K}\widehat\Phi(z)\widehat\Phi(Az)\widehat\Phi(Bz)
   = Q \sum_{x,y \in K}\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\Phi(Ax+By).
\]
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Expanding the three transforms and multiplying out,
\[
  \widehat\Phi(z)\widehat\Phi(Az)\widehat\Phi(Bz)
   = \sum_{x,y,w \in K}\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\Phi(w)\,
      \psi(zx)\psi(Azy)\psi(Bzw),
\]
and $\psi(zx)\psi(Azy)\psi(Bzw) = \psi\bigl(z(x+Ay+Bw)\bigr)$.  Summing over
$z \in K$ and interchanging sums, the orthogonality relation
$\sum_{z \in K}\psi(zs) = Q$ for $s = 0$ and $0$ for $s \neq 0$ (valid because
$\psi$ is primitive; this is the case $D = 1$ of the computation in
Lemma~\ref{lem:powD}(2)) gives
\[
  \sum_{z\in K}\widehat\Phi(z)\widehat\Phi(Az)\widehat\Phi(Bz)
  = Q\sum_{\substack{x,y,w\in K\\x+Ay+Bw=0}}\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\Phi(w).
\]
In characteristic two the constraint is $x=Ay+Bw$, so the last sum is
$\sum_{y,w}\Phi(Ay+Bw)\Phi(y)\Phi(w)$.  Renaming $(y,w)$ as $(x,y)$ and
reordering the factors proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:symmetrisation}
For all $A,B \in K$,
\[
  \sum_{x,y \in K}\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\Phi(Ax+By)
   = c \sum_{u,v \in \mu_{3}} W_{u,v}(A,B).
\]
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
For $a,b,g \in \mu_{3}$ put
\[
  V(a,b,g) = \sum_{x,y \in K}
     \psi\bigl(a x^{D} + b y^{D} + g (Ax+By)^{D}\bigr),
\]
so that, expanding the three copies of $\Phi$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:VVV}
  \sum_{x,y\in K}\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\Phi(Ax+By)
   = \sum_{a,b,g \in \mu_{3}} V(a,b,g).
\end{equation}
Note that $V(u,1,v) = W_{u,v}(A,B)$.  Fix $b \in \mu_{3}$ and set
$\tau = (b^{-1})^{m} \neq 0$, so $\tau^{D}=b^{-1}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:powD}(1).
The substitution $(x,y)\mapsto(\tau x,\tau y)$ is bijective and gives
\[
  V(a,b,g) = V(ab^{-1},1,gb^{-1}).
\]
For fixed $b$, multiplication by $b^{-1}$ permutes $\mu_{3}$ in both the
first and third coordinates.  Thus
\[
  \sum_{a,g\in\mu_{3}}V(a,b,g)
   = \sum_{u,v\in\mu_{3}}W_{u,v}(A,B),
\]
independently of $b$.  Summing over the $c$ choices of $b$ and using
\eqref{eq:VVV} proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:weil}
Let $u,v \in \mu_{3}$ and $A,B \in K$ with $A^{3}\neq 1$.  Then
\[
  W_{u,v}(A,B)=Q\bigl(R_{u,v}(A,B)-1\bigr).
\]
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
If $u+vA^{D}=0$, cubing gives $(A^{3})^{D}=1$, hence $A^{3}=1$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:powD}(1), a contradiction.  Thus the sum over $x$ in the slice
$y=0$ vanishes by Lemma~\ref{lem:powD}(2).  For $y\neq0$, substitute $x=ty$;
then
\[
  ux^{D}+v(Ax+By)^{D}+y^{D}
   = C(t)y^{D},\qquad C(t)=ut^{D}+v(At+B)^{D}+1.
\]
For fixed $t$, the sum over $y\neq0$ is $Q-1$ if $C(t)=0$ and $-1$ otherwise,
again by Lemma~\ref{lem:powD}(2).  Summing over $t$ gives
$W_{u,v}(A,B)=Q|\{t:C(t)=0\}|-Q$.  Since the characteristic is two,
$C(t)=0$ is equivalent to $ut^{D}+v(At+B)^{D}=1$, proving the formula.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
First, $B \neq 0$: if $B = 0$ then $A^{3} = A^{3}+B^{3} = 1$, contradicting the
hypothesis $A^{3} \neq 1$.  (So the hypothesis $B \neq 0$ need not be
postulated separately.)  Thus $A,B \in K^{\times}$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:eightZ} applies.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:phihatzero} the summand of
$\sum_{z\inK^{\times}}\widehat\Phi(z)\widehat\Phi(Az)\widehat\Phi(Bz)$ vanishes at
$z = 0$ --- indeed already its first factor does --- so the sum over $K^{\times}$ may
be replaced by the sum over $K$.  Chaining
Lemmas~\ref{lem:eightZ}, \ref{lem:parseval}, \ref{lem:symmetrisation}
and~\ref{lem:weil} in this order,
\begin{align*}
  8\,Z(A^{3})\,c
   &= \sum_{z \in K^{\times}}\widehat\Phi(z)\widehat\Phi(Az)\widehat\Phi(Bz)
    = \sum_{z \in K}\widehat\Phi(z)\widehat\Phi(Az)\widehat\Phi(Bz)\\
   &= Q\sum_{x,y \in K}\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\Phi(Ax+By)
    = Q\,c\sum_{u,v \in \mu_{3}}W_{u,v}(A,B)\\
   &= Q\,c\sum_{u,v\in\mu_{3}}Q\bigl(R_{u,v}(A,B)-1\bigr)
    = c\,Q^{2}\Bigl(\sum_{u,v\in\mu_{3}}R_{u,v}(A,B) - c^{2}\Bigr),
\end{align*}
the last step because the index set $\mu_{3} \times \mu_{3}$ has $c^{2}$
elements.  Since $c \ge 1$ we may cancel the factor $c$, and dividing by $8$,
\[
  Z(A^{3}) = \frac{Q^{2}}{8}
    \Bigl(\sum_{u,v \in \mu_{3}}R_{u,v}(A,B) - c^{2}\Bigr),
\]
as asserted.  Note that the hypothesis $A^{3}+B^{3} = 1$ entered only through
$B \neq 0$; it is the normalisation under which the pair $(\rho,\sigma) =
(A^{3},B^{3})$ satisfies $\sigma = 1+\rho$, i.e.\ under which the left-hand
side is the phase triple sum of Definition~\ref{def:slopes}.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:noncube}
Assume the Walsh formula of Theorem~\ref{thm:walshchar}.  If $\rho$ or
$1+\rho$ is not a cube in $K$, then $Z(\rho) = 0$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
If $c = 1$ every element is a cube and there is nothing to prove; so assume
$c=3$, i.e.\ $n$ even, and let (say) $\rho$ be a non-cube.  The cubes form a
subgroup of index $3$ of $K^{\times}$, so for each $\lambda \in K^{\times}$ at least one of
$\lambda$, $\rho\lambda$ is a non-cube; by Lemma~\ref{lem:Snoncube},
$S$ vanishes at non-cubes, so every summand of
$Z(\rho) = \sum_{\lambda}S(\lambda)S(\rho\lambda)S(\sigma\lambda)$ vanishes.
The case where $1+\rho$ is a non-cube is symmetric.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:positivity}
Assume the Walsh formula, let $\rho = A^{3}$ be an admissible cube slope with
$A, B \in K$ and $A \neq 0$ such that $A^{3}+B^{3} = 1$, and suppose that the
following holds:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:solvable}
  \text{for all } p,q \in K^{\times} \text{ with } p^{3}+q^{3}=1
  \text{ there exist } w,z \in K \text{ with } w+z=1,\; w^{m}+p z^{m} = q .
\end{equation}
Then $ Z(\rho) \ge 0$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:phaseroot} it suffices to show
$R_{u,v}(A,B)\ge 1$ for all $u,v \in \mu_{3}$.  Put $a = u^{m}$, $b = v^{m}$;
then $a^{3} = b^{3} = 1$, and $a,b \neq 0$.  Apply \eqref{eq:solvable} to the
target
\[
  p = \frac{bA}{a}, \qquad q = bB,
\]
which is legitimate: $p,q \neq 0$ and
$p^{3}+q^{3} = A^{3}+B^{3} = 1$ because $a^{3}=b^{3}=1$.  We obtain $w,z$ with
$w+z=1$ and $w^{m} = pz^{m}+q$ (recall $-1 = 1$).  Set
\[
  t = \frac{z^{m}}{a} .
\]
Then $t^{D} = \bigl((z/u)^{m}\bigr)^{D} = z/u$, so $u t^{D} = z$.  Moreover
\[
  At+B = \frac{Az^{m}}{a}+B = \frac{1}{b}\bigl(p z^{m} + q\bigr)
       = \frac{w^{m}}{b} = \Bigl(\frac{w}{v}\Bigr)^{m},
\]
whence $(At+B)^{D} = w/v$ and $v(At+B)^{D} = w$.  Therefore
$u t^{D}+v(At+B)^{D} = z+w = 1$, i.e.\ $t$ is a root and
$R_{u,v}(A,B)\ge 1$.  Consequently
$\sum_{u,v}R_{u,v}\ge c^{2}$ and $Z(\rho) = \tfrac{Q^{2}}{8}(\sum R_{u,v}-c^{2})$
is a nonnegative real number.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:rootexistence}
Let $|K| = 2^{n}$, $\gcd(k,n)=1$ and $2^{k}+1 = 3m$, and in the even case also
$\gcd(m,2^{n}-1)=1$.  Then $\mathrm{RootEqSolvable}(m,K)$ holds: for all
$p,q \in K^{\times}$ with $p^{3}+q^{3}=1$ there are $w,z \in K$ with $w+z=1$ and
$w^{m}+pz^{m}=q$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:hessian}
For two affine Fermat points $(w_{1},t_{1})$, $(w_{2},t_{2})$ define the
Hessian quantities
\[
  D_{0} = w_{1}t_{1}+w_{2}t_{2},
  \qquad
  N_{x} = t_{1}^{2}w_{2}+t_{2}^{2}w_{1},
  \qquad
  N_{y} = w_{1}^{2}t_{2}+w_{2}^{2}t_{1}.
\]
\begin{enumerate}
  \item The quantities $D_0$, $N_x$, and $N_y$ vanish simultaneously if and only if $(w_1,t_1) \boxminus (w_2,t_2)$ is a point at infinity.
  \item An affine Fermat point is $3$-torsion if and only if one of its coordinates vanishes. 
  \item If $D_{0}\neq 0$ then
  \[
    (w_{1},t_{1}) \boxplus (w_{2},t_{2})
    = \Bigl(\frac{N_{x}}{D_{0}},\ \frac{N_{y}}{D_{0}}\Bigr)
  \]
  in the group $E(K)$.  
  \item Inversion and doubling are given by
  \[
    \boxminus (w,t) = (t,w),\qquad [2](w,t) = (t^4, w^4).
  \]
  \item Translation by a point at infinity $P_{a} = (1:a:0)$ is
  \[
    (w,t)\boxplus P_{a} = (aw,\ a^{2}t) \qquad (a^{3}=1),
  \]
  and $P_{a} \in E[3]$ for every $a$ with $a^{3}=1$.  
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
All assertions follow by direct computation using the formulas above with affine coordinates $(w_i,t_i)=(X_i/Z_i,Y_i/Z_i)$ of $P_i$ for $i=1,2$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:frobfacts}
\begin{enumerate}
\item (CM relation) $\pi^{2} = [-2]$ on $E(L)$ for every field $L \supseteq
      \mathbb{F}_{2}$ of characteristic two.
\item $\ker(1+\pi)$ consists exactly of the three points at infinity
      $P_{a}$, $a^{3}=1$, over any field of characteristic two.
\item If $|K| = 2^{n}$ then $\pi^{n} = \mathrm{id}$ on $E(K)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
(1) follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:hessian}(4) for affine Fermat points. Points at infinity are 3-torsion and defined over $\mathbb{F}_4$, hence fixed by $[-2]$ and $\pi^2$.  (2) Working with homogeneous coordinates,
$(1+\pi)(X:Y:Z) = O$ means $\pi(X:Y:Z) = \boxminus(X:Y:Z) = (Y:X:Z)$, i.e.\ there is
$c \neq 0$ with $X^{2} = cY$, $Y^{2}=cX$, $Z^{2}=cZ$.  If $Z \neq 0$ then
$c = Z$, so $X^{4} = Z^{2}Y^{2} = Z^{3}X$, i.e.\ the affine coordinates
$x = X/Z$ and $y = Y/Z$ satisfy $x^{4}=x$ and $y^{4}=y$, hence lie in $\mathbb{F}_{4}$
and have cubes in $\{0,1\}$.  The affine equation $x^{3}+y^{3}=1$ then forces
$x = 0$ or $y = 0$; but $x = 0$ gives $X = 0$ and then $ZY = X^{2} = 0$, so
$Y = 0$ as well, contradicting $x^{3}+y^{3}=1$, and symmetrically for $y=0$.
Hence $Z=0$, and conversely every point at infinity is in the kernel.  (3) Every coordinate of a $K$-rational point
satisfies $x^{2^{n}} = x$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:twisted}
Let $W,T$ be nonzero elements in the algebraic closure of $K$ with $W^{3}+T^{3}=1$, let $\gcd(k,n)=1$, suppose
\[
  \pi^{n}\mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{Q} \boxplus P_{\alpha} \quad\text{for some } \alpha^{3}=1
  \qquad (\mathcal{Q} = (W,T)),
\]
and suppose $\Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q})$ is not $3$-torsion.  Then $\Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q})$ is an affine
Fermat point $(p,q)$ with $p,q \neq 0$ and
\[
  W^{2^{k}+1} + p\,T^{2^{k}+1} = q .
\]
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:reduction-to-phi}
Suppose that for every affine Fermat point $(p,q)$ of $E$ with $p,q\neq 0$
there exists an affine $\mathcal{Q} = (W,T)$, defined over some extension of $K$ but with
$W^{3}, T^{3} \in K$, such that $W,T \neq 0$, the Frobenius twist relation
$\pi^{n}\mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{Q}\boxplus P_{\alpha}$ holds for some $\alpha^{3}=1$, and
$\Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q}) = (p,q)$.  Then $\mathrm{RootEqSolvable}(m,K)$ holds.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Given a target $(p,q)$, take $\mathcal{Q}=(W,T)$ as in the hypothesis; $\Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q}) =
(p,q)$ is not $3$-torsion since $p,q\neq 0$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:twisted}
gives $W^{2^{k}+1}+pT^{2^{k}+1} = q$.  Put $w = W^{3}$, $z = T^{3}$.  Then
$w+z = W^{3}+T^{3} = 1$, and since $3m = 2^{k}+1$,
\[
  w^{m} + p z^{m} = W^{3m}+pT^{3m} = W^{2^{k}+1}+pT^{2^{k}+1} = q .
\]
Both $w$ and $z$ lie in $K$ by hypothesis, so the pair $(w,z)$ witnesses
solvability.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:tw-weighted}
For every affine Fermat point $(W,T)$ and every $k$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted}
  W^{2^{k}+1}\,N_{y} \;+\; N_{x}\,T^{2^{k}+1} \;=\; D_{0}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Since $W^{2^{k}+1} = AW$ and $T^{2^{k}+1} = BT$, the left-hand side equals
\[
  AW\bigl(W^{2}B+A^{2}T\bigr) + \bigl(T^{2}A+B^{2}W\bigr)BT
   = ABW^{3} + A^{3}WT + ABT^{3} + B^{3}WT .
\]
Grouping the first with the third and the second with the fourth term,
\[
  AB\bigl(W^{3}+T^{3}\bigr) + WT\bigl(A^{3}+B^{3}\bigr) = AB + WT = D_{0},
\]
by the two Fermat equations.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:tw-unfold}
Let $\alpha^{3}=1$.  Then $\pi^{n}\mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{Q}\boxplus P_{\alpha}$ if and only if
\[
  W^{2^{n}} = \alpha W \quad\text{and}\quad T^{2^{n}} = \alpha^{2}T .
\]
In that case $(WT)^{2^{n}}=WT$, $\bigl(W^{3}\bigr)^{2^{n}} = W^{3}$, and
$\bigl(T^{3}\bigr)^{2^{n}} = T^{3}$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:hessian}, $\mathcal{Q}\boxplus P_{\alpha} = (\alpha W, \alpha^{2}T)$,
while $\pi^{n}\mathcal{Q} = (W^{2^{n}}, T^{2^{n}})$; two affine Fermat points are equal
exactly when their coordinates agree, whence the stated equivalence.  Cubing
the two coordinate identities and using $\alpha^{3}=1$ gives
$(W^{3})^{2^{n}} = (W^{2^{n}})^{3} = \alpha^{3}W^{3} = W^{3}$ and
$(T^{3})^{2^{n}} = \alpha^{6}T^{3} = T^{3}$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:tw-nodegen}
Let $W,T \neq 0$, $\gcd(k,n)=1$, and assume the twist relation
$\pi^{n}\mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{Q}\boxplus P_{\alpha}$ for some $\alpha^{3}=1$.  Then
$D_{0} = N_{x} = N_{y} = 0$ is impossible.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Assume for contradiction that 
  \begin{align*}
    D_{0} &= WT + AB = WT + W^{2^k}T^{2^k} = 0, \\
    N_{x} &= T^{2}A + B^{2}W = T^2W^{2^k} + T^{2^{k+1}}W = 0, \\
    N_{y} &= W^{2}B + A^{2}T = W^2T^{2^k} + W^{2^k}T^2 = 0.
  \end{align*}
  Applying Lemma \ref{lem:tw-unfold} and $\gcd(n,k)=1$, we obtain $WT=(WT)^2$. Since $WT \neq 0$, this implies $WT = 1$. But then
  \[ 
    N_{x} = W^{2^k-2} + W^{-2^{k+1}+1} = 0,
  \]
  equivalently, $W^{3(2^k-1)}=1$. Combining this with $(W^3)^{2^n-1}=1$, we get $W^3=1$. Then $T^3=1+W^3=0$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:tw-nonvanishing}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:twisted} we have
\[
  D_{0} \neq 0, \qquad N_{x} \neq 0, \qquad N_{y} \neq 0 .
\]
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lem:tw-nodegen}, $D_{0} = N_{x} = N_{y} = 0$ is impossible. By Proposition~\ref{prop:hessian}, these are the homogeneous coordinates of the affine Fermat point $\mathcal{Q}\boxplus \pi^{k}\mathcal{Q}$. If one of them were zero, then $\mathcal{Q}\boxplus \pi^{k}\mathcal{Q}$ would be $3$-torsion, and then
\[
  [3](\Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q})) = [3](\boxminus(\mathcal{Q}\boxplus\pi^{k}\mathcal{Q})\boxplus T_3) = [-3](\mathcal{Q}\boxplus\pi^{k}\mathcal{Q}) \boxplus [3]T_3 = O,
\]
contradicting the assumption that $\Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q})$ is not $3$-torsion.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
The projective coordinates of the sum $\mathcal{Q}\boxplus \pi^{k}\mathcal{Q}$ are given by $(N_{x}:N_{y}:D_{0})$, and all three coordinates are nonzero by Lemma~\ref{lem:tw-nonvanishing}. We can use the Hessian addition laws to compute $\Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q}) = \boxminus(\mathcal{Q}\boxplus \pi^{k}\mathcal{Q})\boxplus T_{3}$ in these coordinates.
Indeed, $\boxminus(N_{x}:N_{y}:D_{0}) = (N_{y}:N_{x}:D_{0})$, and adding
$T_{3} = (1:0:1)$ by the projective formulas gives
\[
  \Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q}) = (N_{x}^{2} : N_{x}D_{0} : N_{x}N_{y}) = (N_{x}:D_{0}:N_{y}),
\]
using $N_{x} \neq 0$.
This means that $\Phi_k(\mathcal{Q})$ is an affine point with coordinates $(p,q)$, where 
\[
  p = \frac{N_{x}}{N_{y}} \neq 0, \qquad q = \frac{D_{0}}{N_{y}} \neq 0.
\]
Divide the weighted identity \eqref{eq:weighted} of Lemma~\ref{lem:tw-weighted} by $N_{y} \neq 0$:
\[
  W^{2^{k}+1} + \frac{N_{x}}{N_{y}}\,T^{2^{k}+1} = \frac{D_{0}}{N_{y}},
  \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad
  W^{2^{k}+1} + p\,T^{2^{k}+1} = q . \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
It is worth recording where each hypothesis is spent. The assumption that
$\Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q})$ is not $3$-torsion is what rules out the two degenerate
configurations, $D_{0}=0$ (the two points sum to a point at infinity) and
$N_{x}N_{y}=0$ (the sum is an affine $3$-torsion point).  The twist relation
$\pi^{n}\mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{Q}\boxplus P_{\alpha}$ together with $\gcd(k,n)=1$ and $W,T \neq 0$ is
used exactly once, in Lemma~\ref{lem:tw-nodegen}, to exclude the totally
degenerate case in which all three Hessian quantities vanish.  In that case
$W^{3}$ and $T^{3}$ are fixed by $\pi^{k}$, and the twist relation makes them
fixed by $\pi^{n}$ as well; it is only the coprimality of $k$ and $n$ that then
pushes them into the prime field and produces the contradiction.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:oddkernel}
Let $|K| = 2^{n}$ with $n$ odd and $\gcd(k,n)=1$.  Then a point of $E(K)$ lies
in $\ker(1+\pi^{k})$ if and only if it is the origin.  Consequently
$1+\pi^{k}$ is a bijection of the finite group $E(K)$, and hence so is the map
$\Phi_k(P)=\boxminus((1+\pi^k)P)\boxplus T_3$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
As in Proposition~\ref{prop:frobfacts}(2), the kernel condition on a
homogeneous triple $(X:Y:Z)$ reads: there is $c\neq 0$ with
$X^{2^{k}} = cY$, $Y^{2^{k}} = cX$, $Z^{2^{k}} = cZ$.  If $Z \neq 0$ then
$c = Z^{2^{k}-1}$ and one computes that the affine coordinate $x = X/Z$
satisfies $x^{2^{2k}} = x$; since also $x^{2^{n}} = x$ and
$\gcd(2k,n) = \gcd(2,n) = 1$ for odd $n$, Bézout gives $x^{2} = x$, so
$x \in \{0,1\}$.  The kernel equations also give $y=x^{2^{k}}=x$, so
$x^{3}+y^{3}=0$, contradicting the affine Fermat equation $x^{3}+y^{3}=1$.
$Z = 0$ and the point is at infinity, $(1:\omega:0)$ with $\omega^{3}=1$;
 the kernel condition becomes $\omega^{2^{k}} = \omega^{2}$.  For odd $n$ the
 only cube root of unity
in $K$ is $\omega = 1$ (as $\gcd(3,2^{n}-1)=1$), giving the origin.  Injectivity of $1+\pi^{k}$ on the finite abelian group
$E(K)$ follows, hence bijectivity, and $\Phi_{k}$ is the composition of
$1+\pi^{k}$ with a negation and a translation.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Let $(p,q)$ be a target, $p,q \neq 0$, $p^{3}+q^{3}=1$; it is an affine Fermat
point $P$ of $E(K)$, not $3$-torsion by
Proposition~\ref{prop:hessian}.  By Proposition~\ref{prop:oddkernel} there is a
unique $\mathcal{Q} \in E(K)$ with $\Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q}) = P$.  $\mathcal{Q}$ is not $3$-torsion:
$\Phi_{k}$ maps $E[3]$ into $E[3]$, whereas $P$ is not $3$-torsion.  In
particular $\mathcal{Q}$ is not a point at infinity, so it is an affine Fermat
point $(W,T)$, and $W,T \neq 0$ by the torsion criterion of
Proposition~\ref{prop:hessian}.  Since $\mathcal{Q}$ is $K$-rational,
$\pi^{n}\mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{Q}\boxplus P_{1}$, so the Frobenius twist hypothesis holds with
$\alpha = 1$, and $W^{3},T^{3}\in K$ trivially.  Corollary
\ref{cor:reduction-to-phi} concludes.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:factor}
Let $k = 2r+1$ be odd with $2^{k}+1 = 3m$.  There are integers $a,b$ with
\[
  a+2b = 1, \qquad a-b = (-2)^{r}, \qquad a^{2}+2b^{2} = m ;
\]
explicitly $b = (1-(-2)^{r})/3$ and $a = (1+2(-2)^{r})/3$.  Set
$G = a - b\pi$ and $H = a+b\pi$, acting on any abelian group equipped with an
endomorphism $\pi$ satisfying $\pi^{2} = [-2]$.  Then
\[
  (1+\pi)\circ G = 1 + \pi^{k},
  \qquad
  H \circ G = G \circ H = [m] .
\]
If moreover some integer $M$ annihilates the group and $\gcd(m,M)=1$, then $G$
is bijective.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
The integrality of $a,b$ follows from $(-2)^{r}\equiv 1 \pmod 3$; the three displayed
identities are then direct computations, using $a^{2}+2b^{2} =
\bigl((a+2b)^{2}+2(a-b)^{2}\bigr)/3 = (1+2\cdot 4^{r})/3 = (2^{k}+1)/3 = m$.
For the factorisation, $\pi^{2}=[-2]$ gives $\pi^{2r} = [(-2)^{r}]$, so
$1+\pi^{k} = 1+(-2)^{r}\pi = (1+\pi)(a-b\pi)$ once $a+2b=1$ and
$a-b = (-2)^{r}$.  The norm identity gives $HG = [a^{2}+2b^{2}] = [m]$.
Finally, if $M$ annihilates the group and $\gcd(m,M)=1$, Bézout provides
integers $s,t$ with $sm+tM = 1$, so $[m]$ is invertible (with inverse $[s]$)
and $G$ is bijective with inverse $[s]H$.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:annihilator}
Let $|K| = 2^{n}$ with $n$ even, and put $c_{n} = (-2)^{n/2}$ and
$\mathcal N = c_{n}-1$.  Then $c_{n}^{2} = 2^{n}$, $\mathcal N \mid 2^{n}-1$,
and $\mathcal N$ annihilates $E(K)$.  If $\gcd(m,2^{n}-1)=1$ then
$\gcd(\mathcal N, m) = 1$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
$c_{n}^{2} = (-2)^{n} = 2^{n}$ since $n$ is even, and
$2^{n}-1 = (c_{n}-1)(c_{n}+1)$, giving the divisibility.  On $E(K)$,
$\pi^{n} = \mathrm{id}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:frobfacts}(3), while
$\pi^{n} = (\pi^{2})^{n/2} = [(-2)^{n/2}] = [c_{n}]$ by the CM relation; hence
$[\mathcal N] = [c_{n}]-\mathrm{id} = 0$ on $E(K)$.  Coprimality is inherited
from $\mathcal N \mid 2^{n}-1$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:Gbij}
Let $n$ be even, $k$ odd, $|K| = 2^{n}$, $2^{k}+1 = 3m$, and
$\gcd(m,2^{n}-1)=1$.  Then $G = a-b\pi$ is a bijection of $E(K)$; in
particular every $R \in E(K)$ has a $K$-rational preimage $Y$ with
$G(Y) = R$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Combine Lemmas~\ref{lem:factor} and~\ref{lem:annihilator}.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:quotient}
Let $L$ be a field of characteristic two and let $(x,y)$ be an affine point of
$x^{3}+y^{3}=1$ with $x,y\neq 0$.  Let $W \in L$ satisfy
$W^{3} = \dfrac{x+1}{x+y}$ and put
\[
  T = \frac{1}{W}\cdot\frac{1+x+y}{x+y}.
\]
Then
\[
  T^{3} = \frac{y+1}{x+y},
  \qquad W^{3}+T^{3} = 1,
\]
and the Hessian data of the pair $(W,T)$, $(W^{2},T^{2})$ satisfy $D_{0}\neq 0$
and
\[
  \frac{N_{x}}{D_{0}} = x, \qquad \frac{N_{y}}{D_{0}} = y ,
\]
i.e.\ $(W,T)\boxplus \pi(W,T) = (x,y)$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
All statements are rational identities in $x,y$ once $W^{3}$ is substituted,
using $x+y\neq 0$, $1+x+y\neq 0$ (both consequences of the cubic equation and
$x,y \neq 0$), and the key identity $1+(x+y)^{3} = (x+y)xy$.  For $T^{3}$:
\[
  T^{3} = \frac{(1+x+y)^{3}}{(x+y)^{3}}\cdot\frac{x+y}{x+1}
        = \frac{(1+x+y)^{3}}{(x+y)^{2}(x+1)} = \frac{y+1}{x+y},
\]
the last step being the polynomial identity
$(1+x+y)^{3} = (y+1)(x+1)(x+y)$ modulo $x^{3}+y^{3}+1$ in characteristic two.
Then $W^{3}+T^{3} = \frac{(x+1)+(y+1)}{x+y} = 1$.  For the Hessian data put
$s = WT = (1+x+y)/(x+y)$, so $1+s = 1/(x+y)$.  Then
$D_{0} = WT + W^{2}T^{2} = s(1+s) \neq 0$,
$N_{x} = T^{2}W^{2} + T^{4}W = WT^{2}(W+T^{2})$, and
$N_{y} = W^{2}T^{2} + W^{4}T = W^{2}T(T+W^{2})$, whence
\[
  \frac{N_{x}}{D_{0}} = \frac{s + T^{3}}{1+s} = \frac{x/(x+y)}{1/(x+y)} = x,
  \qquad
  \frac{N_{y}}{D_{0}} = \frac{s + W^{3}}{1+s} = \frac{y/(x+y)}{1/(x+y)} = y .
\]
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Let $(p,q)$ be a target, and let $P = (p,q) \in E(K)$ be the corresponding
affine Fermat point; $P$ is not $3$-torsion.

\emph{(1) Invert $G$ over $K$.}  Put $R = T_{3}\boxminus P \in E(K)$.  By
Corollary~\ref{cor:Gbij} there is $Y \in E(K)$ with $G(Y) = R$.

\emph{(2) $Y$ is affine with nonzero coordinates.}  $R$ is not $3$-torsion,
since $T_{3}$ is and $P$ is not; and $G$ maps $3$-torsion to $3$-torsion, so
$Y$ is not $3$-torsion either.  Hence $Y = (x,y)$ with $x,y \neq 0$
by Proposition~\ref{prop:hessian}.

\emph{(3) Lift through the degree-three quotient.}  Let $\overline{K}$ be an algebraic
closure of $K$ and regard $(x,y)$ in $E(\overline{K})$ via the base-change homomorphism
$E(K)\to E(\overline{K})$.  Choose $W \in \overline{K}$ with
$W^{3} = (x+1)/(x+y)$ and let $T$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient}; then
$\mathcal{Q} = (W,T) \in E(\overline{K})$ satisfies $\mathcal{Q}\boxplus \pi \mathcal{Q} = (x,y)$.

 \emph{(4) Reassemble the factorisation.}  Base change commutes with $\pi$,
 and $G$ is a polynomial in $\pi$, hence commutes with
$1+\pi$ and with base change.  Therefore, in $E(\overline{K})$,
\[
  (1+\pi)\bigl(G(\mathcal{Q})\bigr) = G\bigl(\mathcal{Q}\boxplus \pi \mathcal{Q}\bigr) = G\bigl((x,y)\bigr)
    = R = T_{3}\boxminus P,
\]
and by Lemma~\ref{lem:factor}, $(1+\pi^{k})\mathcal{Q} = (1+\pi)G(\mathcal{Q}) = T_{3}\boxminus P$, i.e.
\[
  \Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q}) = \boxminus(1+\pi^{k})\mathcal{Q} \boxplus T_{3} = P .
\]

\emph{(5) Control the Frobenius defect.}  $\mathcal{Q}$ itself need not be
$K$-rational, but $\mathcal{Q}\boxplus \pi \mathcal{Q} = (x,y)$ is, hence is fixed by $\pi^{n}$.  Since
$\pi^{n}$ commutes with $1+\pi$,
\[
  (1+\pi)\bigl(\pi^{n}\mathcal{Q} \boxminus \mathcal{Q}\bigr) = \pi^{n}(\mathcal{Q}\boxplus \pi \mathcal{Q})\boxminus(\mathcal{Q}\boxplus \pi \mathcal{Q}) = O,
\]
so $\pi^{n}\mathcal{Q}\boxminus \mathcal{Q} \in \ker(1+\pi)$, which by
Proposition~\ref{prop:frobfacts}(2) is the set of the three points at infinity.
Thus $\pi^{n}\mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{Q} \boxplus P_{\alpha}$ for some $\alpha$ with $\alpha^{3}=1$: the
Frobenius twist hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:twisted} holds.  Also
$W,T \neq 0$, since $\Phi_{k}(\mathcal{Q}) = P$ is not $3$-torsion.

\emph{(6) Descend the invariant cubes.}  Theorem~\ref{thm:twisted}, applied
over $\overline{K}$, gives $W^{2^{k}+1}+pT^{2^{k}+1} = q$.  Setting $w = W^{3}$,
$z = T^{3}$ we get $w+z=1$ and $w^{m}+pz^{m} = q$ as in
Corollary~\ref{cor:reduction-to-phi}.  Finally $w$ and $z$ lie in $K$: by
Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient} they equal $(x+1)/(x+y)$ and $(y+1)/(x+y)$
respectively, which are rational expressions in the $K$-rational coordinates
$x,y$.  No fixed-field descent theorem is needed --- the cube root $W$ was
chosen only \emph{after} the $K$-rational data $w,z$ had been written down.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:forcing}
Let $s$ be a nonempty finite index set, $Q>0$, $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and let
$N_{i} = c + Z_{i}/Q$ with $Z_{i}\ge 0$ for all $i \in s$.  If
$\frac{1}{|s|}\sum_{i\in s} N_{i} = c$, then $N_{i} = c$ and $Z_{i}=0$ for
every $i \in s$.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Summing the hypothesis, $\sum_{i}N_{i} = |s|c + \bigl(\sum_{i}Z_{i}\bigr)/Q$,
while the average condition gives $\sum_{i}N_{i} = |s|c$.  Hence
$\sum_{i}Z_{i}=0$ with all $Z_{i}\ge 0$, so each $Z_{i}=0$ and $N_{i}=c$.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:slopeform}
Let $|K| = 2^{n}$, $1\le k<n$, $k$ odd, $\gcd(k,n)=1$, $2^{k}+1 = 3m$,
$\gcd(m,2^{n}-1)=1$, and $2|\Delta_{k}| = Q$.  Then
\[
  N(\rho) = \frac{Q^{2}}{8} \qquad \text{for every admissible } \rho .
\]
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Let $D$ be an inverse of $m$ modulo $N = |K^{\times}|$; 
note $m \neq 0$ and $\mathcal S \neq \emptyset$ because
$n \ge 2$.  Theorem~\ref{thm:phase}
gives the phase formula, and Theorem~\ref{thm:walshchar} converts it into the
all-character Walsh formula for $S$, the Walsh transform of $\Delta_{k}$.

\emph{Pointwise lower bound.}  Let $\rho$ be admissible.  If $\rho$ or
$1+\rho$ is not a cube, then $Z(\rho) = 0$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:noncube}.
Otherwise write $\rho = A^{3}$, $1+\rho = B^{3}$ with $A,B \in K$; then
$A \neq 0$ (as $\rho \neq 0$), $A^{3}+B^{3} = \rho + 1 + \rho = 1$, and
$A^{3} = \rho \neq 1$.  Theorem~\ref{thm:rootexistence} supplies
$\mathrm{RootEqSolvable}(m,K)$ --- through the odd branch if $n$ is odd and
through the even branch if $n$ is even --- so Corollary~\ref{cor:positivity}
gives $ Z(\rho)\ge 0$.

\emph{Conclusion.}  By Theorem~\ref{thm:walshcount},
$N(\rho) = Q^{2}/8 +  Z(\rho)/Q$ for every admissible $\rho$, and by
Theorem~\ref{thm:average} the average of $N$ over $\mathcal S$ is exactly
$Q^{2}/8$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:forcing}, with $c = Q^{2}/8$ and $Z_{\rho} =
 Z(\rho)$, yields $N(\rho) = Q^{2}/8$ for every admissible $\rho$ (and, as a
by-product, $Z(\rho) = 0$ throughout: the Fourier correction vanishes
identically).
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Let $K$, $n$, $k$, $v_{1}$, $v_{2}$ be as in the statement.  By
Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction}, $n \ge 2$ and we may replace $k$ by
$r = k\bmod n$, which satisfies $1\le r<n$ and $\gcd(r,n)=1$, without changing
$N_{k}(v_{1},v_{2})$.

By Result~\ref{res:halfsize}, $2|\Delta_{r}| = Q$.  By
Proposition~\ref{prop:normparam} choose $k_{0}\in\{r,n-r\}$ odd, coprime to
$n$, with $2^{k_{0}}+1 = 3m$ and $\gcd(m,2^{n}-1)=1$; note $1 \le k_{0}<n$.  By
Proposition~\ref{prop:transport} (used only if $k_{0} = n-r$) there are
distinct nonzero $w_{1},w_{2}$ with
$N_{r}(v_{1},v_{2}) = N_{k_{0}}(w_{1},w_{2})$, and by
Result~\ref{res:halfsize} again $2|\Delta_{k_{0}}| = Q$.

Theorem~\ref{thm:slopeform} applies at the parameter $k_{0}$ and gives
$N(\rho) = Q^{2}/8$ for every admissible slope.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:coefslope},
$N_{k_{0}}(w_{1},w_{2}) = Q^{2}/8$, and by \eqref{eq:mainterm} this equals
$2^{2n-3}$.  Chaining the equalities,
\[
  N_{k}(v_{1},v_{2}) = N_{r}(v_{1},v_{2}) = N_{k_{0}}(w_{1},w_{2}) = 2^{2n-3},
\]
which is the assertion.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The proof yields more than the count.  The forcing step shows that the Fourier
correction $Z(\rho)$ vanishes for every admissible slope, and, through
Theorem~\ref{thm:phaseroot}, that for even $n$ and every admissible slope
$\rho = A^{3}$ with $1+\rho = B^{3}$ the twisted root counts satisfy
$\sum_{u,v\in\mu_{3}}R_{u,v}(A,B) = 9$ exactly, i.e.\ each twisted fibre
contains exactly one root; for odd $n$ the corresponding statement is
$R_{1,1}(A,B) = 1$.  The geometry alone gives ``at least one''; exactness comes
from the conserved average.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
